To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TODs have a positive influence on the use of public and active modes, and a negative influence on the use car/taxi.
urban TODs have a positive influence on the use of public transportation and the reduction of car usage.

urban TODs and activity centre TODs are the most effective types of TOD for promoting public transport and reducing car usage; TADs are “evil twins” of TODs; and TOD policy should also include context-specific design principles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the commuting mode choice of people living in TODs and TADs and how this can be enhanced.
the commuting behaviour of the people living in different types and sizes of TODs, TADS and traditional neighbourhoods.

the identification of the commuting mode choice behaviours of people living in different neighbourhoods and the disentanglement of the effects of their TADs, travel attitudes and residential self-selection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TODs are not only about location, but also about design.
TOD policy should not be implemented in TADs.
TODs are a good idea, but TADs are not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TOD policy should focus on the development and implementation of context specific TOD design guidelines, and that the transition of TAD to TODs should be prioritised.
TODs are a success, TADs are an underutilised opportunity, and traditional suburbs should be avoided.
TODs are not the panacea for all of our transport problems, and TADs are not the “evil twin”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TODs are a good way to reduce car usage and increase public transport use, but that TADs can be just as good as TODs, and that TADs need to be transformed into TODs.
TODs are not just a transport planning issue, but rather they should be seen as a planning issue.
TODs are not a one size fits all solution.
